title: Generative AI as a Tool or Leader? Exploring AI-Augmented Thinking in Student Programming Tasks
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how generative AI (GAI) shapes students’ thinking processes during programming tasks, with a particular focus on learner agency: whether students use AI as a tool to support their thinking or allow AI to lead the problem-solving process. The authors note that while prior work has examined the benefits and risks of tools like ChatGPT in programming education, little research has empirically analyzed how students actually think and act while programming with GAI. The study addresses three questions: how to categorize AI-augmented thinking in programming, how human-led and AI-led students differ, and how factors such as attitudes toward AI, critical thinking, and programming self-efficacy relate to these thinking processes.

The study develops and applies an AI-augmented thinking framework based on screen-recording analysis of students completing programming tasks with access to GAI tools such as ChatGPT. The framework includes four stages: Question Formulation, Solution Development, Solution Analysis and Evaluation, and Solution Refinement. Students were grouped as human-led or AI-led according to the ratio of time spent generating their own code versus copying code from AI. The researchers combined qualitative coding of 2,297 events from screen recordings with quantitative analyses including t-tests, sequential pattern mining, and Pearson correlations, making the study both descriptive and correlational.

Participants were 20 students from a single university in Singapore: 10 undergraduates in an engineering computation course and 10 master’s students in a learning analytics course. All had limited prior programming experience. The study took place out of class in an individual one-hour programming session supported by GAI, preceded by a survey on attitudes toward AI, critical thinking, and programming self-efficacy, and followed by reflection reports from most participants. Undergraduate students completed Python programming tasks; graduate students completed an R-based data analysis assignment.

The main findings are that human-led students spent significantly more time on solution development and solution refinement than AI-led students, and their interaction patterns showed more critical engagement with AI outputs. Human-led students commonly checked outcomes, read AI responses, and then manually refined code, whereas AI-led students more often copied AI-generated code and immediately ran it. Positive attitudes toward AI, critical thinking, and programming self-efficacy were positively associated with question formulation, while critical thinking was also positively related to solution refinement. The authors conclude that student agency is central in AI-supported programming: GAI is most beneficial when used as a support for human thinking rather than a substitute for it.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI system used for natural-language interaction, including generating programming code, explanations, debugging help, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: University students used ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools during one-hour programming tasks to ask for source code, explanations, debugging help, and to support problem solving; the paper particularly discusses ChatGPT as the exemplar tool in programming education.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods observational study of 20 university students, students classified as human-led spent significantly more time than AI-led students on Solution Development (t=2.12, p=0.05) and Solution Refinement (t=2.48, p=0.03) while using ChatGPT/GAI during programming. Sequential patterns suggested human-led students more often checked outcomes, read AI answers, and manually refined code, whereas AI-led students more often copied AI-generated code and ran it directly.
findings.measure: Time spent in coded AI-augmented thinking dimensions and frequent sequential behavior patterns from screen recordings

findings.finding_summary: Positive attitudes toward AI, critical thinking, and programming self-efficacy were positively correlated with Question Formulation during ChatGPT/GAI-supported programming (r=0.32, r=0.33, and r=0.39, respectively). Critical thinking was also positively related to Solution Refinement (r=0.47).
findings.measure: Pearson correlations between learner characteristics and coded AI-augmented thinking dimensions

findings.finding_summary: Programming self-efficacy was strongly negatively correlated with Solution Analysis and Evaluation in ChatGPT/GAI-supported programming (r=-0.54). The authors interpret this as more confident programmers spending less time analysing and evaluating AI answers.
findings.measure: Pearson correlation between programming self-efficacy and Solution Analysis and Evaluation

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample mixed-methods observational study with t-tests, sequential pattern mining, and correlations, not an RCT or strong quasi-experiment. Findings are informative but causal claims about effectiveness are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports significant behavioral/process differences and moderate-to-strong correlations, but no direct learning-performance effect size for programming outcomes. Overall impact on student outcomes is promising but unclear.
